short: A decisive engagement that reunited the kingdom of England with the Duchy of Normandy.
full:
On 28 September 1106, the forces of King Henry I of England engaged the army of his older brother, Robert Curthose, outside the castle of Tinchebray in Normandy. The brothers had been in conflict since their father's death divided his territories. Henry's army, bolstered by contingents from Brittany and Maine, broke Robert's lines in a short but decisive battle that lasted barely an hour.

The victory resulted in the capture of Robert, who was imprisoned in various English and Welsh castles for the remaining twenty-eight years of his life. Tinchebray extinguished the threat of a rival Norman court and reunited England and Normandy under a single ruler for the first time since 1087. The dual realm required Henry to spend much of his reign crossing the Channel, driving the development of a highly delegated administration in England.
